## The four o’clock toast

I finished my last night shift on Sunday morning. Saturday 7 November, 21:00 to 07:30, in majors. Fourteen years of nights, and then I went home.

From Monday I’m on a days-only rota. This is good news. My knees think so. My GP, who has stopped finding my approach to my blood pressure even faintly amusing, thinks so. I’m hoping that eventually my sleep will agree.

I thought I would feel straightforwardly pleased. Instead I’ve been trying to write this and finding that everything comes out either as an obituary or a complaint about the NHS. Nobody has died in this particular story. I’m still going to work. And I’ve written enough about what’s wrong with the service to be reasonably sure that another thousand words from me won’t have it sorted by Thursday.

But I don’t quite know how to finish doing something that has occupied fourteen years of my life without saying something about it.

This blog has been neglected since spring. Apparently this is what it takes to get me back to it: a sensible change to my working arrangements, about which I am being surprisingly unsensible.

***

My first night as an SHO was in 2012. I can remember very little about the actual shift now. What I remember from that first winter is crying in the car park at the Infirmary because I couldn’t remember whether I had given a second dose.

I had. That part was checked. There wasn’t an error.

I still remember the frost on the windscreen.

I was tired and frightened by the possibility that being conscientious might not be enough to keep me from making a mistake. I don’t think that fear is unusual among junior doctors, although it can feel very private when you’re sitting in a cold car with it.

Over the years I became more experienced. I got better at making decisions, asking for help, knowing what could wait and what couldn’t. I also got better at recognising when tiredness was making a straightforward problem feel impossible. Sometimes the useful intervention was another pair of eyes. Sometimes it was something to eat.

Nights gave me a lot of my education. Some of it was medicine. A great deal of it came from nurses who knew considerably more than I did and were kind enough to teach me without making that the main subject of the conversation.

Folasade, our charge nurse on nights, has been doing them for twenty-two years. She still beats me up the stairs. I would like to attribute this entirely to my knees, but I suspect she would have beaten me in 2012 as well.

I will miss working nights with her. There isn’t a more elaborate way of putting that which improves on it.

***

People tend to think nights in emergency medicine are about adrenaline. There is some of that, obviously. But it doesn’t account for most of the hours, or for what makes someone good to work with.

Mostly, it’s about staying kind at five in the morning when you are empty.

It’s explaining something again without letting the person hear that you have already explained it several times. Remembering that someone who seems unreasonable may be frightened, in pain, or having the worst night they can remember. Not taking your tiredness out on a colleague who is just as tired and has asked a perfectly reasonable question.

I haven’t always managed it. There are conversations I would conduct differently if I could have them again after eight hours’ sleep and breakfast. I don’t want to turn nights into a test of character that I conveniently passed.

But I’ve worked with people who managed that kindness so consistently that it changed what I expected of myself.

I think the department is most itself at night. There are fewer managers about, which won’t be a controversial observation to anyone who works there. People are often more direct. There is less energy available for pretending everything is fine, and sometimes that makes it easier to ask for help.

There is a particular kindness, too. Not universal, not guaranteed, but familiar enough that I will miss it. Someone noticing you haven’t sat down. Someone taking over for a few minutes without requiring a full explanation of why you need them to.

And the toast.

At about four in the morning, someone always makes toast in the staff room. Nobody admits to starting it. I have never established whether there is a system, and after fourteen years it seems late to begin an investigation.

You smell it before you get there. On some nights it’s the first time you’ve realised you’re hungry. You eat it and talk, or don’t talk, and for a little while nobody needs you to know anything.

I’m aware that I’m describing toast as though it were a significant professional benefit. At four in the morning, it is.

***

There are moments with patients that I will keep, though most aren’t mine to put on a blog.

Once, during a night shift, someone held my hand and told me I had their daughter’s hands.

I’ve thought about that often. I didn’t have anything particularly useful to say in reply. I stayed for a moment. In a job where so much of your attention goes towards what you need to do next, I’m glad I didn’t immediately move on.

That is as much of that story as belongs here.

***

Nights took things as well.

I missed both my nieces’ naming ceremonies. There was meant to be video, a way of being there from Leicester when I couldn’t be in Bangalore. Nights got in the way of that too.

My sister never once complained.

I don’t want to turn her generosity into evidence against myself. She understood. But I still missed them, and understanding doesn’t give you an occasion back.

There were other things, less memorable individually: days that were technically free but spent recovering, conversations I was too tired to follow properly, plans made on the optimistic assumption that this time I would wake up feeling human.

For years I treated recovery as something I ought to be able to get more efficient at. Better curtains, better timing, a slightly different arrangement of meals and sleep. Some of those things helped. None of them made me someone who didn’t need to sleep at night.

Now I’m forty-two. My knees hurt, my sleep isn’t good, and my blood pressure needs taking seriously. I’m moving to days partly because I would like to feel better, and partly because continuing to hope my body will get used to it seems a poor clinical plan.

I’m relieved.

I also feel like a traitor for being relieved. I know how that sounds. If a colleague told me the same thing, I’d tell them to take the days-only rota and look after themselves. I would mean it, without qualification. I’m finding it harder to extend that entirely ordinary advice to myself.

Nobody has accused me of abandoning anything. This is my own contribution to the leaving arrangements.

***

On Sunday morning I drove home down the London Road as the sun was coming up. I had the Radio 4 shipping forecast on catch-up, which is perhaps an unnecessarily complicated relationship with time even for someone coming off nights.

I realised I wouldn’t see that light from this side again.

I’ll be awake at that hour, of course. I’ll drive to early shifts. The sun will continue to rise over Leicester without reference to my rota. But I won’t be seeing it after working through the whole night, with the department still going round in my head and bed waiting at the other end of the journey.

I hadn’t expected to mind losing that view. I did.

I’m looking forward to things as well. More ordinary evenings. Being properly awake when I speak to my sister. Finding out how much better I might feel after a few months of not repeatedly turning my sleep upside down. I might even write here again before another season passes.

I don’t need to decide that nights were either wonderful or terrible before I’m allowed to stop doing them. They gave me colleagues I trust, taught me how to be a doctor, and cost me more than I was always willing to admit. I’m glad I did them. I’m glad I’m stopping. It may take a while for those two things to sit comfortably together.

Meanwhile, Folasade will still be getting up the stairs faster than people who ought to be able to keep up with her. There will be people on their first winter of nights, learning who to ask and when to ask them.

I hope they get a few minutes to sit down at four.

Someone will have made toast.
